issues.legal_issue: Identification of accused persons is established where they were named in the earliest account, were known to the witnesses, and witnesses later identified their presence and participation.
material_facts: The accused were named in the earliest account of the occurrence and were co-villagers known to the witnesses.
The witnesses later named the accused and attributed presence and participation to them.
The accused did not challenge their identification during the investigation or at trial.
issues.conclusion: The identification challenge was without substance.
issues.legal_principle: Identification is assessed in the circumstances of the case. Here, naming the accused in the earliest account, the witnesses’ prior familiarity with them, and later testimony identifying their participation supported the finding of identification.

rule.if: criminal_appeal_from_conviction and accused_named_in_earliest_account and accused_known_to_witnesses and witnesses_later_identified_participation and identification_not_challenged

predicates.criminal_appeal_from_conviction: The matter is an appeal from a criminal conviction.
predicates.accused_named_in_earliest_account: The accused were named in the earliest account of the occurrence.
predicates.accused_known_to_witnesses: The accused were already known to the witnesses.
predicates.witnesses_later_identified_participation: Witnesses later named the accused and described their presence and participation.
predicates.identification_not_challenged: The accused did not challenge their identification during the investigation or at trial.

issues.definition: When an appeal from a conviction concerns accused named promptly, known to the witnesses, and later identified as participants without an identification challenge, their identification is established.

issues.legal_issue: Consistent eyewitness evidence supported by medical evidence is not discredited merely because independent witnesses were not examined or forensic corroboration was unavailable.
material_facts: Six eyewitnesses gave a consistent account of the occurrence.
The informant was seriously injured in the occurrence, and his presence was not in doubt; he gave an account soon after the incident.
Medical evidence showed numerous injuries, including firearm injuries, consistent with the eyewitness account.
No independent village witness was examined, and the investigating officer did not recover pellets from the open field or obtain a ballistic report.
issues.conclusion: The absence of independent witnesses and the missing forensic corroboration did not provide a reason to doubt the prosecution case.
issues.legal_principle: The court may rely on credible, consistent eyewitness testimony, particularly when it is supported by medical evidence; the absence of independent witnesses or particular forensic evidence does not by itself require rejection of that testimony.

rule.if: criminal_appeal_from_conviction and consistent_eyewitness_account and medical_evidence_supports_account and (independent_witnesses_not_examined or forensic_corroboration_unavailable)

predicates.criminal_appeal_from_conviction: The matter is an appeal from a criminal conviction.
predicates.consistent_eyewitness_account: The eyewitnesses gave a consistent account of the occurrence.
predicates.medical_evidence_supports_account: Medical evidence was consistent with the account given by the eyewitnesses.
predicates.independent_witnesses_not_examined: No independent witness was examined to support the prosecution account.
predicates.forensic_corroboration_unavailable: Relevant forensic corroboration, such as recovered projectiles or a ballistic report, was unavailable.

issues.definition: In an appeal from a conviction, consistent eyewitness evidence supported by medical evidence is not discredited solely because independent witnesses or forensic corroboration are absent.

issues.legal_issue: Unexplained injuries to accused persons do not undermine the prosecution case when the defence has not established that the injuries arose in the same occurrence and at the same place.
material_facts: Some accused persons had injuries that the prosecution did not explain.
The defence offered no counter-version identifying where or how the injuries occurred and did not claim self-defence.
The injuries were not fatal and did not threaten life.
issues.conclusion: The prosecution case could not be disbelieved because of the accused persons’ unexplained injuries.
issues.legal_principle: The prosecution’s obligation to explain injuries to an accused depends on establishing that the injuries were sustained in the same occurrence and at the same place. In the absence of that foundation or a plea of self-defence, and where the injuries are not serious, their non-explanation does not require rejection of the prosecution case. The court distinguished Lakshmi Singh v. State of Bihar (1976) 4 SCC 394 and Siri Kishan v. State of Haryana (2009) 12 SCC 757 on their facts.

rule.if: criminal_appeal_from_conviction and accused_sustained_unexplained_injuries and not same_occurrence_and_place_established and no_counter_version and no_self_defence_claim and injuries_not_serious

predicates.criminal_appeal_from_conviction: The matter is an appeal from a criminal conviction.
predicates.accused_sustained_unexplained_injuries: One or more accused persons had injuries that the prosecution did not explain.
predicates.same_occurrence_and_place_established: The defence established that the accused persons sustained their injuries in the same occurrence and at the same place.
predicates.no_counter_version: The defence did not provide a counter-version explaining where or how the injuries occurred.
predicates.no_self_defence_claim: The defence did not claim that the injuries arose while acting in self-defence.
predicates.injuries_not_serious: The injuries were not fatal and did not threaten life.

issues.definition: In an appeal from a conviction, unexplained injuries to accused persons do not discredit the prosecution when their connection to the same occurrence and place is unestablished, no counter-version or self-defence claim is made, and the injuries are not serious.

issues.legal_issue: Members of an unlawful assembly may be held liable for offences committed in prosecution of its common object, including where the common object forms during the occurrence.
material_facts: A group of five or more persons chased and attacked the victims, killing four people and grievously injuring another.
The group’s conduct during the occurrence demonstrated a common object to commit serious offences.
The accused were found to have been members of the assembly when the offences were committed.
issues.conclusion: The courts below correctly applied the law of unlawful assembly to uphold convictions for murder and attempted murder with the aid of the rule of collective liability.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 141 and 149 of the Indian Penal Code require an unlawful assembly of five or more persons and liability for an offence committed in prosecution of its common object, or an offence the members knew was likely to be committed in prosecution of that object. The incriminating act must serve the common object or be within the members’ knowledge as a likely act: Kuldip Yadav v. State of Bihar (2011) 5 SCC 324. Common object is assessed from the circumstances, conduct and weapons of the assembly: Roy Fernandes v. State of Goa (2012) 3 SCC 221. It may form on the spur of the moment without prior concert: Ramchandran v. State of Kerala (2011) 9 SCC 257.

rule.if: criminal_appeal_from_conviction and assembly_of_five_or_more and accused_member_when_offence_committed and conduct_shows_common_object_to_commit_offence and offence_in_prosecution_of_common_object_or_known_likely

predicates.criminal_appeal_from_conviction: The matter is an appeal from a criminal conviction.
predicates.assembly_of_five_or_more: Five or more persons acted together as an assembly.
predicates.accused_member_when_offence_committed: The accused was a member of the assembly when the offence was committed.
predicates.conduct_shows_common_object_to_commit_of: The assembly’s conduct showed a common object to commit an offence.
predicates.offence_in_prosecution_of_common_object_: The offence was committed in prosecution of the common object or was known by the assembly members to be likely in prosecution of that object.

issues.definition: A person who is a member of an assembly of at least five persons when an offence is committed may be held liable for it if the assembly’s common object encompassed the offence or its commission was known to be likely in pursuing that object.

issues.legal_issue: In a mass-offence case, an individual conviction requires adequate, clear corroboration of the evidence identifying the accused as a participant.
material_facts: The case involved many accused and victims, and the accused and material eyewitnesses were co-villagers.
The court considered the witnesses’ identification of each accused individually.

For five accused, fewer than three witnesses clearly identified the particular accused as a participant; in one instance, witnesses who used the same name did not distinguish between two people with that name.
issues.conclusion: The five accused whose individual participation was not supported by clear evidence from three witnesses were entitled to the benefit of doubt and were acquitted.
issues.legal_principle: For an offence involving a large number of offenders and victims, the normal test is that conviction should be supported by two or more witnesses giving a consistent account: Masalti v. State of Uttar Pradesh, AIR 1965 SC 202, as applied in Busi Koteswara Rao v. State of Andhra Pradesh (2012) 12 SCC 711. The court applied a three-witness expectation in this case because the accused and eyewitnesses were co-villagers. The court also cautioned against relying on general testimony that does not identify an accused or specify that person’s role.

rule.if: criminal_appeal_from_conviction and mass_offence_case and witnesses_and_accused_are_co_villagers and fewer_than_three_clear_witness_identifications

predicates.criminal_appeal_from_conviction: The matter is an appeal from a criminal conviction.
predicates.mass_offence_case: The case concerns an offence involving a large number of alleged offenders and victims.
predicates.witnesses_and_accused_are_co_villagers: The eyewitnesses and accused persons are from the same village or are similarly familiar with one another.
predicates.fewer_than_three_clear_witness_identific: Fewer than three witnesses clearly identified the particular accused as a participant, including where witnesses did not distinguish between people with the same name.

issues.definition: In a mass-offence appeal involving witnesses and accused who are familiar with one another, an individual conviction is not sustained and benefit of doubt is given when fewer than three witnesses clearly identify that accused as a participant.

issues.legal_issue: A lack of clear motive does not undermine a conviction proved by clear and cogent evidence.
material_facts: The appellants disputed whether a clear motive had been established.
The court found that the offences were proved by clear and cogent evidence, including eyewitness testimony.
issues.conclusion: Motive was not necessary or material to the convictions in light of the proof of the offences.
issues.legal_principle: Where an offence is established by clear and cogent evidence, including reliable eyewitness evidence, proof of motive is not necessary to sustain the conviction.

predicates.criminal_appeal_from_conviction: The matter is an appeal from a criminal conviction.
predicates.clear_cogent_evidence_proves_offence: Clear and cogent evidence, including eyewitness evidence, proves the offence.
predicates.motive_not_established: The prosecution has not established a clear motive.

issues.definition: In an appeal from a conviction, the absence of an established motive does not undermine the conviction when clear and cogent evidence proves the offence.
